title: Prajna Paramita in Eight Thousand Lines
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer invites listeners to cultivate awareness and compassion by letting go of attachments and ego, embracing the present moment without preconceptions or expectations. By doing so, we can live in the world with full enjoyment and appreciation, free from entanglements and misunderstandings about reality. This approach is likened to the practice of a bodhisattva, who goes forth into the world with love and awareness, cultivating compassion and kindness in each moment.

sentences.text: *Call forth as much as you can of love, of respect, and of faith. [unclear: "Move"] the obstructing defilements and clear away all your taints.
Listen to the perfect wisdom of the gentle Buddhas taught for the wheel of the world or heroic spirits intended.*
That's the opening verse of the Prajna Paramita Sutra in 8,000 lines.
Can you hear better?
Yeah?
It's funny, depending on where you're sitting, probably some of you can hear very well, right?
I had that problem yesterday.
Maybe we'll get more volume here.
So it looks like several of you in the back can't hear, right?
I'll read that again.
It's a beautiful verse.
I've been impressed with it ever since I heard it a long time ago.
*Call forth as much as you can of love, of respect, and of faith.
Remove the obstructing defilements and clear away all your taints.
Listen to the perfect wisdom of the gentle Buddhas taught for the wheel of the world or heroic spirits intended.*
So, good morning everybody.
Nice to see you.
Very, very nice to be here at Samish.
Another year with everyone.
I'm always astounded to show up and find so many of you here.
Sesshin is pretty counter-cultural.
It's not what most people do.
So it's amazing that all of us here have somehow decided that despite that, it makes sense to us anyway to be here and spend a week in this way.
It's so hard to find a week, right?
You could be in Hawaii or somewhere having fun or doing something productive.
So it's amazing that this many people would think that it makes sense for them to come and do this.
According to Buddha Dharma, it is highly likely that the reasons you think you have for being here are not the real reasons.
According to Buddha Dharma, it is most probable that there are other, probably deeper and less personal, reasons than the ones you think you have.
And perhaps you will eventually discover those reasons.
Maybe even this week you'll discover those reasons.
This is like pretty much everything in our lives that we think we have chosen, when the truth is we have been chosen.
Everything and everyone has chosen us and here we are.
And as Tim told us so wonderfully in such a lively way yesterday, we are here to be together and, hand in hand, enter into the miracle of sesshin together.
And yes, it takes some effort, some organizing effort to begin with, to make this happen.
And also the effort that we're all going to make every single day until the end.
It's a funny kind of effort because we have to really, really relax, maybe in a way that we have not learned to relax before.
And at the same time we have to pay close attention all the time.
That's the part that we have to do.
So there's some effort on our part.
But the rest of it is not up to us.
And I think you come to see this in sesshin pretty clearly, but it's true actually all the time in your life.
Our lives really are not ours and they never have been.
And what happens in our lives is really not the result of what we do and it never has been.
Of course we have our part to play.
We all have to make a big effort just getting through the day, from breakfast till climbing into bed takes a big effort.
So we have our part to do.
But our lives are not our fault and they don't belong to us.
This is liberating to know.
This means you don't have to worry about anything anymore.
Anything you're worried about is extra.
Believe me, all you have to do is make a joyful effort to pay attention and to be generous and kind, and the rest will take care of itself.
And to live that way is a tremendous pleasure.
So now I have to say Happy Father's Day, because today is Father's Day.
So Happy Father's Day to all the fathers in the room, and whether or not you are a father, you had a father or have a father, right?
To me this is so astonishing and surprising.
Everybody, everybody has a father and a mother.
You'd think statistically there would be exceptions, right?
Like 85% of people would have fathers, 92%.
But it seems, as far as I can tell, there may be some exceptions but I never really have heard of any.
Everybody without exception has a father and a mother.
To be a father, to have or to have had a father and a mother, this is really something.
This is very mysterious.
We will never understand it.
And the older I get, the more amazed I am by the resonance, the texture of these deep human relationships.
Freud was right about this.
He was right that these relationships really run deep.
But even before Freud, the Bible already was telling you how bewildering and complicated these relationships are.
And I think, as everybody here can well appreciate, it is pretty much impossible to get these relationships right.
It's just not going to happen.
They usually go haywire, one way or the other, to some degree or another.
Sometimes they go very badly indeed.
So I hope if you are a father or if you had or have a father, this is not the case for you.
I hope that you have had a relationship that has gone on the whole pretty well.
Anyway, however well or not well it's gone, you have the rest of your life and beyond to try to make it better, regardless of whether your father is still alive.
So all this is just to say Happy Father's Day to everybody here.

Maybe some day, during the day, it will spontaneously or intentionally occur to you to spend a moment or two thinking of your father with gratitude and amazement, no matter what kind of father he was.
*Call forth as much as you can of love, of respect, of faith.
Remove the obstructing defilements and clear away all your taints.
Listen to the perfect wisdom of the gentle Buddhas.
Talk for the wheel of the world for heroic spirits intended.*
Wheel.
We don't use this word too much.
Talk for the [unclear: "wheel"] of the world.
Wheel means welfare, well-being, benefit.
Like we have the word common [unclear: "wheel"].
Or the word common wealth.
Or the word wealthy, which now comes to mean having lots of money and lots of property and lots of stuff.
But actually it doesn't mean that.

It means having enough material goods for well-being but also having a sense of community and belonging and a healthy point of view and a sense of being in the world with wheel, with benefit and well-being.
So in the very beginning the Sutra tells us that the teaching here is not for our enlightenment, not for our understanding or our mystical experiences or making our lives better.
It's taught for the wheel of the world.
All of us together.
That's the teaching.
That's why it's given: to benefit the world.
And it's intended for heroic spirits, courageous spirits, because it takes courage and heroism to see life clearly and to live life fully for the wheel of the world.
So this teaching would be for heroic spirits.

After that opening stanza, which we could, our whole practice could just be that opening stanza, the text goes on to speak about the basic teachings of perfect wisdom, which is the subject of this Sutra.
*No wisdom can we get hold of.
No highest perfection.
No Bodhisattva.
No thought of enlightenment either.
When told of this, if not bewildered and in no way anxious, a Bodhisattva courses in the well-gone's wisdom.*
The well-gone being an epithet for the Buddha.
*Courses in the well-gone's wisdom.
In form and feeling, will, perception and awareness, nowhere in them they find a place to rest on.
Without a home they wander.
Dharmas never hold them nor do they grasp at them.
The Jainas Bodhi they are bound to gain.*
Jaina is another epithet for the Buddha.
It means conqueror.
So these are the opening lines that describe the teaching of the Sutra.
The first point in the basic teaching is there is no basic teaching.
There is no Prajnaparamita.
It's just like Tim was saying yesterday, it's all just talk.
That's what it's saying.
It's just talk, just words, just an idea that doesn't have anything behind it.

So this is the first and most basic teaching: there is no Prajnaparamita, there is no transcendent wisdom, there are no Bodhisattvas, there are no heroic spirits, there is no thought of enlightenment either.
Thought of enlightenment is the usual and literal translation of the word Bodhicitta.
Bodhicitta, which is the sort of shining centerpiece of Bodhisattva practice.
It's the shining moment of entry into the Bodhisattva path experienced by every Bodhisattva.
It's the moment when you recognize that there is no other way, there is no other choice that anyone can make other than to fully and completely enter the path for and with others.
Bodhicitta is the moment when it dawns on you that your life of isolation and struggle is a big misunderstanding and that you cannot go on that way anymore, and that in fact no one can.

The fact that religion exists at all, and that it has motivated so many billions and billions of people, providing them a basis for living for so many, many, many generations, really since the beginning of humanity, tells us that Bodhicitta is an indelible part of being human.
It's something that exists in all of us, and when we get in touch with it our lives are from that moment on completely altered, even if from the outside they may appear the same.
And the text says, yes, and actually there is no such thing as Bodhicitta.

So when we hear all this, there is no perfect wisdom, there are no Bodhisattvas, there is no Bodhicitta, if we hear all this and we don't get freaked out and baffled and confused, and instead feel perfectly happy about it, then we know we are walking on the Buddhist path.
That's what the text is saying.
*In form, in feeling, will, perception and awareness, nowhere in them they find a place to rest on.
Without a home they wander.
Dharmas never hold them nor do they grasp at them.
The Jain is Bodhi they are bound to gain.*
The reason Bodhisattvas don't get upset when they hear that there is no perfect wisdom, no Bodhisattvas and no thought of enlightenment is because they know what that means.
It doesn't mean that these things do not exist.
Also it doesn't mean that these things do exist.
Because dharmas are empty, as we chant every morning, this means there is no actual existence.
Existence is a kind of exaggeration, it's like an extreme view.
And there is no actual non-existence either, because non-existence is also an exaggeration, an extreme view.
What we think we have we don't really have.
Who we think we are, we really aren't that person.
So what we think we are going to lose we can't actually lose, because we never had it to begin with.
That's why the Heart Sutra says there is no birth and death and there is no extinction of birth and death.
We are passing the Han going to the meals, and the Han says, "Birth and death, the great matter."
Great matter means birth and death are beyond birth and death.
Birth and death is much greater than birth and death, and it is vitally important for us to realize this if we are ever going to figure out how to live together peacefully with some happiness.
Things exist and not at the same time.
You and I literally, exactly, exist and don't at the same time.
We are all the time appearing and disappearing, which makes it possible for us to grow, to develop.
Amazing.

All our friends, if they would notice that we are appearing and disappearing at the same time and constantly different, if they would let us be different, if they would see how we are changing, they would be amazed.
We would be amazed.
So we know that this is what the sutra is telling us, so we don't get baffled and scared and freaked out.
We are really happy about it because it means we are free and we have nothing to worry about.
Having no place to rest, inside or outside, doesn't mean that we are restless, looking around here and there for a place to land.
It means we are free inside and out, and freedom is the opposite of isolation and selfish choice.
It means we are free to love everything.
We are free to flow in and out of everything.
We are free to live and die joyfully.
So it doesn't freak us out or make us scared when we hear that we aren't anything or anyone and that we don't have anything.
We have no identities.
Fabulous.
Our identities are [unclear: "wonderful mixed"] that we tell one another.
Otherwise how are we going to meet each other?
How are we going to interact with each other if we don't say, "I'll tell you my story, you tell me yours"?
A fabulous story: "What happened to me, you can't believe it."
Yes, that's how we make friends, that's how we meet.
We never did have any identities anyway, or anything else.
So we are not really tragically giving something up.
The only thing we are giving up is our unhappiness, our confusion, our loneliness.
That's okay, we can give that up.
The next verse says:
*The wanderer Shrenika in his gnosis of truth could find no basis though the skandhas had not been undone.
Just so the Bodhisattva, when she comprehends the dharma as she should, does not retire into blessed rest.*
Shrenika was an ascetic who came to the Buddha and in meeting the Buddha understood the perfection of wisdom.
*when he couldn't find any actual basis for anything, and he saw that everything is free of itself.* It says he saw this though the skandhas had not been undone.
In other words, *like the bodhisattva he did not retire into blessed rest, into nirvana.* This is very astonishing when you think about the implications.
It means that when we come to sesshin, we are not coming to gain some insight or understanding so that we can end our suffering.
That would be undoing the skandhas, retiring into blessed nirvana.
When we study the early Buddhist sutras, the Buddha seems to be telling us to end suffering and enter nirvana.
Here the speaker of these lines, Subhuti, who we are told in an earlier verse speaks the mind of the Buddha, is telling us something that appears to be quite different.
He is telling us not to undo our entanglements, because that is what the five skandhas are: our human life, our entanglements.
Don't undo your entanglements.
Don't slough off your entanglements and enter nirvana, leaving them all far behind.
Instead, dwell in perfect wisdom that neither exists nor doesn't exist.
Thanks to this perfect wisdom, now we can live in the five skandhas with full and deep enjoyment but without being caught by them.
We don't need to run away from them, because there is nothing to run away from.
Instead of dwelling in nirvana, the bodhisattva dwells in perfect wisdom.
The next verse says:
*In wisdom then he dwells.
What is this wisdom, whence and [unclear: "whos"] he queries, and then he finds that these dharmas are entirely empty.
Uncowed and fearless in the face of that discovery, not far from bodhi, awakening, is that bodhisattva.

Bodhi being then to course in the skandhas, in form and feeling and perception, will and so on, and to fail precisely or to imagine these skandhas as being empty means to course in a sign, the track of non-production ignored.

But when he does not course in form and feeling or perception, in will or consciousness, but wanders without home, remaining unaware of coursing, firm in wisdom, his thoughts in non-production, then the best of all the calming trances cleaves to him.

Though that bodhisattva now dwells tranquil, tranquil in himself, his future buddhahood assured by antecedent buddhas, whether absorbed in trance or whether outside of trance he doesn't mind, for of things as they are he knows the essential original nature.
Thus he courses in the wisdom of the sugatas, the buddhas, and yet he does not apprehend the dharmas in which he courses.
This coursing he wisely knows as no coursing.
That is his practice of wisdom, the highest perfection.*
*What exists not, that non-existent, the foolish imagine.
Non-existence as well as existence they fashion as dharmic facts.
Existence and non-existence are both not real.
A bodhisattva goes forth when wisely he knows this.*
So the bodhisattva is committed to continue to course in this entangled world, but she considers it with wisdom.
She knows it's not as it seems to be, nor does she turn around and imagine now that she's got it figured out: "Aha, all dharmas are empty.
Got it."
That would be going too far.
That's what it says.
That would be making empty dharmas into something, into a sign, a technical term that means more or less something that can be apprehended and grasped, and boom, we're caught all over again.
No.

The bodhisattva lives this entangled life with some amazement, some appreciation, some equanimity, always willing to be surprised all over again and willing to undergo whatever needs to be undergone, without making everything into a religious dogma.
When she lives like this, it says she's actually practicing meditation all the time, the best kind of meditation, the kind that doesn't have any particular signs, like being calm, being peaceful.

It can be calm and peaceful, and in fact, in a way that's not marked by outward signs, it's always calm and peaceful, even though outwardly it can seem sometimes like agitation, if agitation is called for.
Or it can look very energetic, if energy is called for.
It can even look like unhappiness and dissatisfaction, but it remains at bottom peaceful, because the bodhisattva knows what is going on.

She knows that she is only and always wandering in the middle of nowhere, with no possessions, nothing to hold onto, nothing to do or think, simply making the effort to respond appropriately and always with love.
She's probably not saying or thinking, "Look at me, I'm wandering, I'm floating, I'm accepting everything with love."
She's probably not saying that.
She's probably not thinking that.
As it says, she's not thinking like that.
If she starts thinking like that, she starts thinking, "What an idiot, what am I thinking?"
She's not thinking like that, but she is holding her life tenderly and with wonder.
She's willing not to know what's going on, and she's open to [unclear: "greet her"] and she knows it could be something good, it could be something not too good.
Whatever it is, I'm here.
And yet, as it says, *and yet he doesn't apprehend the dharmas in which he courses.* He doesn't apprehend the dharmas in which he courses.
This is what I'm saying.
It's the main point, through all the perhaps boring scholastic language about existing, non-existing and all this.
This is the point in Zen teaching, which is always so much more simple and pithy.
There's a koan that Cathy and I were considering when we were at Upaya a couple months ago, a very simple Zen story.

The monks are always asking, on Taishan, an old tea lady is by the road there, they're always asking her what's the way to Mount Taishan, and she always says to each and every one of them, "Right straight ahead."

That's our practice: right straight ahead, facing forward, facing this ineffable moment which we don't understand, where anything could happen, and simply doing what needs to be done, resting in what needs to be done all the time.
We really don't think we're practicing Zen or being peaceful or wise.
As soon as we, you've had this experience, the minute you think, "Ah, this is it," then you trip over something and you smack your head off a tree and you're all screaming and troubles happen.
We all know this.
We don't think we're practicing Zen, we're being wise, we're being peaceful.
We recognize what nonsense all that is.
We don't think we're Zen priests or Zen masters or long-term experienced Zen students who have done this and done that.
We don't think that.
We know all of that is such baloney.
It's just silly.
We can get caught in that in a minute.
Yes, we recognize, okay, we have our roles, our temporary positions.
For five minutes we'll be in this position.
We're going to take our place right here where we're supposed to be, in whatever temporary position we find ourselves in for this moment: a mother, a father, a son, a daughter.
We're going to occupy that position, we're going to do what we can, and we're going to do it completely, for that five minutes, as long as it lasts.
*A bodhisattva goes forth when wisely she knows this.* A bodhisattva goes forth.
This is a phrase: to go forth means to awaken.
To awaken, just going forth, a moment after a moment.
So in this spirit I have a few practical suggestions for you for sesshin.
Maybe they'll help.
When you're sitting, really redouble your commitment to pay very close attention to your body, especially to your posture in sitting.
Somewhere it says, I think maybe in Hakuin's song of zazen, "This very body is the body of Buddha."
That's right.
All these teachings that I've been talking about this morning clearly cannot be realized intellectually, by the mind, by thinking.
There's no question about that, because thinking is always a yes-and-no affair.
That's how thinking operates: it's this and not that.
Prajnaparamita in essence defies that kind of thinking.
It includes it, but it cannot be penetrated with that kind of thinking.
So we need to realize these teachings.
You might be frustrated trying to think them through, but we realize them with our body, our spirit, our heart, beginning always with the body.
So when you sit, pay close attention to five points.
The first point is your butt, your seat, the basis on which the whole Buddha body is upheld.
So sit firmly on your seat.
Be careful when you sit down, and notice how you're sitting there.
There are two little sit bones in your butt.
Notice those two sit bones.
Now I think that most of us sit a little too far forward.
We're leaning a little too far forward in our seats.
So when you pay attention to those two sit bones, feel the pressure back further behind on your butt.
That's going to make you lean back.
You might think you're leaning too far back, but experiment with it.
Feel your weight further back on those sit bones than you think is right.
This will make your back lean back a little more, and it might feel odd at first, but it's actually free.
It frees the body.
So that's the first point: your butt, your seat.
The second point is your mudra.
Feel your thumb tips just touching, and feel the gentle curve in the palms of your hands.
Feel how delicate and beautiful a thing it is when those thumb tips are just touching.
It's actually a beautiful feeling inside, and it looks beautiful when the palms are curved and the thumb tips are just touching.
As much as you can, as you sit, keep your attention on the mudra.
Don't lose track of it, and feel literally a sense of beauty.

Wouldn't that be something, to be able to feel the beauty of your own hands held in the mudra, and to have your whole body inspired by the beauty of this just-right, just-so feeling of the thumb tips touching?
It will make your whole body feel full of ease and beauty.
The third point is your belly.
Feel your belly soft and free.
Feel it gently going in and out with your breathing.
Feel the breathing low and deep and steady and strong in your belly, and let it just be like that.
Don't force anything.
Just let it come and go in that way, and begin to feel how every breath pervades the whole body, wakes up and relaxes the whole body.
The fourth point is the sternum, right here, lifting and opening.
This feeling should come from the inside.
From the inside you should feel your body lifting and opening.
You're not imposing.
This is the thing: we don't even know we're doing this, but we're imposing our lives on ourselves.
We've got something like a tyrant in there telling us, "You've got to be like this."
That same guy gets in there when we're practicing.
Quiet, forget about it, go home, wherever you live.
Don't let that person impose some fake Zen baloney on your body.
Let your body, from the inside, open, because that's what it wants to do.
It wants to lift, it wants to open.
This is the Buddha body, the dignified human body.
It wants to lift, it wants to open.
Let that happen.
Don't force it, let it happen.
So pay attention here.
This is the heart area, right?
When you lift and open here, your feeling lifts and opens.
The last point follows from that one.
Allow a lifting here.
There's a lifting here, the back part of your head.
You can feel it pressing up toward the sky, lifting, rising up.

It should feel like up far away in one of the heavens the Buddha is suspending a gossamer thread down, and it just clicks right here on top of your head, gently, very gently pulling you up, and you can feel yourself held up, lifted up.
So that's lots to pay attention to, right?
You don't need to do anything else but just pay attention to these five points: your seat, your mudra, your belly, your sternum, the top of your head.
I don't mean this as some kind of assignment, and I certainly don't mean it as something now you have more things to worry about.
No, but gently and easily, if you want to, you can practice these points.
If you do, I think it will help your sitting a lot.
It will open your heart and your whole body a lot.
And the whole time, not only when you're sitting, always, always practice paying attention with your body.

When you're standing up, when you're sitting in the dining hall, during the work period, when you're walking anywhere, not just in kinhin but anytime, when you lie down, when you stretch, always return attention to the body over and over again.
Feel how kind, generous and reliable your body is, how patient with you your body is.
Your body is the best friend you'll ever have.
It keeps you company forever and ever, and if it's complaining, there's a reason for that.
So pay loving attention every day, all day long, to your body.
Sesshin is a wonderful quiet drama.
All of us are the authors and the actors and the stage managers and the producers.
So thanks to everyone for sharing this wonderful practice together.
It's beautiful.

*Call forth as much as you can of love, of respect and of faith, without any obstructing defilements, and clear away all your taints and listen to the wisdom of the gentle buddhas taught for the wheel of the world, for heroic spirits intended.*
Thank you.
